name: Sara Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Sara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any tech company, employer, union or political party, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fenwick's, which has been selling houses in our market town for over sixty years. We do village houses, old cottages, the odd farmhouse, and some lettings. I spend the mornings on the phone and the afternoons driving out to viewings down lanes the sat-nav doesn't know. Mr Fenwick still knows half the families in the area by name, and that's what people come to us for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's hard about it for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Valuing the old properties. A cottage with a thatched roof and no proper foundations is a puzzle, and I still get it wrong. And the computer side, honestly, I avoid it where I can. Margaret, who's run the office for thirty years, does the uploads for me, bless her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people buy from people, and that's how it should be. At church and with friends I'd say I always thought it was overblown. I don't do much online, so I wouldn't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Fenwick's would carry on, and I could keep learning from Mr Fenwick at my own pace. Daniel and I own our little cottage with a small mortgage, and we've got savings, so we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am and spend more time out with Mr Fenwick on valuations. We'd carry on planning the wedding next summer and keep saving. I wouldn't change anything on the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled. Like Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid the computer side. Is that a worry for Fenwick's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. Margaret retires in a few years and someone will have to do the uploads. I suppose that would be me, and I'd have to learn, but slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the chains. The big agency in the next town undercuts our fees every year. That's a worry for my boss Mr Fenwick whatever happens with computers.

say: I'd say **people buy from people**, as it should be.
I'd tell friends at **church** it was overblown.
think: Fenwick's carries on and I **keep learning** at my own pace.
A **small mortgage** and savings mean we're comfortable.
do: **Spend more time** with Mr Fenwick on valuations.
Leave the **computer side** to the office manager.
S0.quote: The big agency in the next town undercuts our fees every year. That's a worry for my boss Mr Fenwick whatever happens with computers.
fieldNote: Her biggest worry in this world is **chain competition**, not AI.
She relies on **Margaret (the office manager)** for all computer work.
Her **faith and family** frame how she talks about work.

steps.text: Go out with Mr Fenwick on every cottage valuation
Keep saving for next summer's wedding with Daniel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there'll always be a place for an agent who knows the area. I'd probably say it a bit defensively at work. At church people would ask me, and I'd say we're not worried at Fenwick's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit. The chains would use AI to cut their fees even further, and Mr Fenwick would have to match them somehow. And if Margaret's job became a computer program, I'd be the one expected to run it, which I'm not good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Fenwick's and finally let Margaret teach me the uploads and the portal, but I'd still avoid anything that writes for me. I'd keep saving and go ahead with the wedding. Daniel's family runs a builders' merchants, so I know there's always work there if I needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground is shifting a little under an old house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid anything that writes for you. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when I describe a cottage, I want it to be true and in my own words. The AI listings from the chains all sound the same, and every kitchen is stunning. Our buyers can tell the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, mostly. She's sixty-two and the office is her life. If the computer does her job, Mr Fenwick would keep her on out of kindness, but she'd know.

say: I'd say there's always room for an agent who **knows the area**.
I'd tell church friends that **Fenwick's** isn't worried.
think: The **chains** would use AI to cut fees further.
If office work becomes software, I'd have to **run it**, badly.
do: **Learn uploads** from Margaret but avoid AI writing tools.
Go ahead with the **wedding** and keep saving.
Remember there's **backup work** at Daniel's family builders' merchants.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the ground **shifting** under an old house.
S1.quote: The AI listings from the chains all sound the same, and every kitchen is stunning. Our buyers can tell the difference.
fieldNote: She'd learn **basic computer tasks** but refuse AI writing tools.
Her concern for **Margaret (the office manager)** is warm and specific.
Daniel's **family business** is her quiet safety net.

steps.text: Learn the property portal uploads from Margaret this year
Go ahead with next summer's wedding and keep saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has been forced on ordinary people by tech companies who never asked anyone. I'd say families and communities need to look after each other, because I don't trust the government to sort it. I'd talk about it at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Fenwick's would close within a couple of years. If AI can value, negotiate and do the paperwork by 2028, the chains would sell houses for almost nothing. Mr Fenwick is sixty-eight, and I don't think he'd fight it, he'd retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the savings safe and stop any big spending. Daniel and I would scale the wedding right down, maybe the church and a meal at the pub instead of the hotel. I'd ask Daniel's dad if there's a job for me at the builders' merchants, serving at the counter or driving deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. And a bit lost, because I always thought I'd do this for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Serving at a builders' merchants is quite a change. How would you feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud enough, honestly. It's honest work and it's family. Daniel's grandad started that yard, and if it keeps us fed, that's what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools if it meant staying in property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. If the job is just checking what a computer says, it isn't the job I chose. I'd rather be lifting bags of cement.

say: I'd say **tech companies** forced this on ordinary people.
I'd say **families and communities** must look after each other.
think: **Fenwick's would close** within a couple of years.
Mr Fenwick at **sixty-eight** would retire rather than fight it.
do: **Stop big spending** and keep savings safe.
**Shrink the wedding** to church and a pub meal.
**Ask Daniel's dad** for a job at the builders' merchants.
S2.quote: If the job is just checking what a computer says, it isn't the job I chose. I'd rather be lifting bags of cement.
fieldNote: She expects her **employer to close** outright.
She turns to **family**, not government, for support.
She'd choose **manual work** over becoming someone who checks an AI's output.

steps.text: Stop all big spending and protect the savings
Scale the wedding down to church and a pub meal
Ask Daniel's dad for counter work at the builders' merchants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so families should plan together. I'd be at church saying the same. I'd still not post much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect Fenwick's to struggle by 2031. Mr Fenwick would be in his seventies, so he might retire anyway. Five years is time to work out the next thing calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Fenwick's while it lasts, and maybe start helping Daniel's family with sales at the yard on Saturdays. We'd have the wedding as planned. I'd think about having children around 2028, so I'm settled before it all changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slower kind. I'd have time to pray on it and talk it through with Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you want children before AGI arrives, rather than after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum always said you never feel ready, you just go. I'd rather have a baby while we still know how things work. And Daniel's family would help, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper apprenticeships, not handouts. If the jobs change, help young people learn a real trade. I don't want to be paid to sit at home.

say: I'd say families should **plan together** with a few years' warning.
I'd talk it through at **church**, not online.
think: Five years is time to work out **the next thing** calmly, with Daniel.
Mr Fenwick might **retire** anyway in his seventies.
do: **Keep working at Fenwick's** while it lasts.
**Help at the yard** on Saturdays, selling to builders.
feel: **Anxious**, but slower and calmer to **think through**.
S3.quote: My mum always said you never feel ready, you just go. I'd rather have a baby while we still know how things work.
fieldNote: She'd bring **family plans** forward rather than delay them.
She wants **apprenticeships**, not handouts, from government.
**Faith and prayer** are part of how she processes change.

steps.text: Keep working at Fenwick's for as long as it stays open
Help with sales at the builders' merchants yard on Saturdays
Try for a first child around 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people to sort themselves out. At work I'd say Fenwick's has seen off worse. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. In ten years I'd likely have a couple of children and be working part-time, maybe at the yard. Fenwick's would probably have gone by then anyway, with Mr Fenwick retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Fenwick's and get better at valuations. We'd have the wedding as planned and save for a bigger house. Around 2030 I'd start working more at Daniel's family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it feels far off. I'd mostly feel settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be working part-time at the yard. Would that be your choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. I want to be home with little ones, like my mum was with us. My job at Fenwick's was always going to be the first part of my life, not all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the AI tools in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if everyone did. But I'd rather learn the trade properly from Mr Fenwick while he's still here. That's worth more to me than a program.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** for people to sort themselves out.
I'd say **Fenwick's** has seen off worse.

Fenwick's might close anyway when **Mr Fenwick retires**.
do: **Improve valuations** at Fenwick's while Mr Fenwick is still there.

Work more at Daniel's **family business** from 2030.

steps.text: Keep learning cottage valuations from Mr Fenwick

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Fenwick's would go and there'd be no time to plan. What would help is proper apprenticeships for young people and support for family businesses, so places like Daniel's yard can take more people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the villages. People out there don't use computers much. If buying a house becomes all screens, the old couples who've lived in the same cottage for fifty years will be the ones who get left behind.

headlineQuote: If buying a house becomes all screens, the old couples who've lived in the same cottage for fifty years will be the ones who get left behind.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old junior agent** at a sixty-year-old market town agency selling cottages and village homes.
She **avoids computers** and never uses AI, relying on the office manager for uploads.
She owns a cottage with her fiancé Daniel, with a **small mortgage** and savings.
Her **traditional views** show in trust in family, church and apprenticeships over government help.
In fast scenarios she'd **turn to Daniel's family** builders' merchants; with time she'd focus on children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Fenwick's would close with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for young people and support for **family businesses**.
